content: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age characterized by hormonal imbalance, ovulatory dysfunction, and often cysts on the ovaries. The exact cause of PCOS remains unclear, but it involves complex interactions among genetic, environmental, and metabolic factors. Key mechanisms include insulin resistance, increased androgen levels (hyperandrogenism), and impaired follicular development. PCOS presents with symptoms such as irregular menstrual cycles, hirsutism (excess hair growth), acne, obesity, and infertility. Diagnosis is typically clinical, supported by laboratory tests and pelvic ultrasound, using criteria such as the Rotterdam criteria. Management of PCOS requires a multidisciplinary approach including lifestyle modifications (diet and exercise), medical therapies targeting insulin resistance, hormonal imbalances, and fertility issues. Evidence supports lifestyle changes as first-line therapy due to benefits in weight reduction and improved metabolic profiles. There are important safety considerations especially with medication use, needing individualized treatment plans. Major synonyms include Stein-Leventhal syndrome and polycystic ovarian disease, but ‘PCOS’ is most widely used. Limitations in current understanding relate to heterogeneous presentation and response to therapy. Accurate patient education and continuous monitoring are necessary for appropriate management. This module provides comprehensive, evidence-calibrated knowledge on PCOS, aimed at patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers.

content: PCOS affects up to 10-15% of women of reproductive age worldwide and is associated with significant impacts on fertility, metabolic health, and quality of life. Understanding its causes, symptoms, and management is essential to improve health outcomes and prevent long-term complications such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

chunk_title: Definition and Diagnostic Criteria of PCOS
content: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is defined by the presence of at least two of the following three criteria according to the Rotterdam consensus: 1) oligo- or anovulation (infrequent or absent ovulation), 2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, and 3) polycystic ovaries visible on ultrasound. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other disorders such as thyroid dysfunction and hyperprolactinemia. The term “polycystic ovaries” describes ovaries with multiple immature follicles but does not alone confirm PCOS.

content: The exact cause of PCOS is multifactorial and not fully understood. It involves genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors such as diet and lifestyle. Major pathophysiological mechanisms include insulin resistance leading to compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which stimulates ovarian androgen production. Elevated androgens disrupt normal follicle development, causing arrested follicle growth and anovulation. Inflammation and altered gonadotropin secretion also contribute to disease manifestations.

chunk_title: Hormonal and Metabolic Changes in PCOS
content: Women with PCOS often exhibit increased serum levels of androgens such as testosterone and androstenedione, decreased sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), and dysregulated luteinizing hormone (LH) to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio. Insulin resistance is prevalent, even in non-obese women, contributing to hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes risk. Metabolic syndrome components such as dyslipidemia and hypertension are more common among PCOS patients.

content: PCOS symptoms vary widely and include menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea), hirsutism (excess facial or body hair), acne, seborrhea, alopecia or thinning hair, obesity, and infertility. Psychological issues such as depression and anxiety are also frequent. Some women may be asymptomatic but diagnosed during infertility evaluation or metabolic screening.

content: Risk factors for PCOS include family history (first-degree relatives with PCOS), obesity, insulin resistance, and exposure to certain environmental factors. Prevalence varies across ethnicities but generally affects 6-15% of women globally. Early menarche and sedentary lifestyle have been associated with increased risk. PCOS is a leading cause of anovulatory infertility in women.

content: Clinical evaluation includes detailed history and physical examination focusing on menstrual cycle pattern, signs of androgen excess, and metabolic risk factors. Laboratory testing typically includes serum total and free testosterone, SHBG, LH and FSH, glucose tolerance testing, lipid profile, and thyroid function tests to exclude other conditions. Pelvic ultrasound assesses ovarian morphology. Diagnosis is based on integrating clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings.

content: Management is individualized based on patient goals such as ovulation induction, symptom control, or metabolic risk reduction. First-line therapy emphasizes lifestyle modification including weight loss, diet, and exercise to improve insulin sensitivity and ovulation. Pharmacologic options include combined oral contraceptives to regulate menses and reduce androgen effects, metformin to improve insulin resistance, and fertility treatments if conception is desired. Anti-androgens may be used in select cases.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Lifestyle interventions are cornerstone treatments for PCOS, especially for overweight or obese patients. A balanced diet focusing on low glycemic index carbohydrates, lean protein, and healthy fats can improve insulin sensitivity and reduce symptoms. Regular moderate exercise enhances metabolic health and aids weight management. Avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol is recommended. Psychological support is vital due to the higher prevalence of anxiety and depression among women with PCOS.

content: Women with PCOS face increased risks of infertility, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, endometrial hyperplasia, and possibly endometrial cancer due to chronic anovulation and unopposed estrogen exposure. Metabolic syndrome components are common, and some evidence suggests an association with sleep apnea and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Early diagnosis and ongoing monitoring can mitigate these complications.

content: Some misconceptions include that all women with PCOS have cysts on their ovaries, that PCOS solely affects obese women, or that it is caused by poor lifestyle choices alone. Not all women with PCOS are infertile, and the condition is not curable but manageable. Myths about instant cure through supplements or diets persist despite limited scientific evidence. Accurate education is essential to reduce stigma and promote effective treatment adherence.

chunk_title: Safety Notes and Monitoring in PCOS Management
content: Safety considerations include monitoring metabolic parameters regularly during treatment, especially when using insulin sensitizers or hormonal therapies. Some medications have contraindications in pregnancy or with certain medical conditions. Weight loss should be gradual and supervised in cases of extreme obesity. Psychological well-being should be assessed periodically. Patients should be informed about potential treatment side effects and importance of follow-up care.
